title: GHG Protocol organisational boundary choices
facts: Three consolidation approaches: equity share (emissions by share of equity, reflecting economic interest), financial control (100% of emissions where the company has financial control) and operational control (100% where it has authority to introduce and implement operating policies).
The choice must be disclosed, not merely made, and applied consistently. Changing it is a structural change that triggers base year recalculation.

Under a control approach a company accounts for none of the emissions of operations it holds an interest in but does not control — which is why two companies can report very different totals for the same joint venture.

title: What a GHG Protocol report must disclose
facts: A reporting company must disclose its organisational boundary including the consolidation approach, its operational boundary including the activity types covered where Scope 3 is reported, and its base year with the recalculation policy and significance threshold.
Gross emissions for the chosen inventory boundary must be presented separately from and independently of any GHG trades or offsets.

Scope 1 and Scope 2 are the minimum. Scope 3 is optional under the Corporate Standard itself — the reason companies report it is usually IFRS S2 paragraph 29(a), ESRS E1-6 or a customer's value chain request, not the Corporate Standard.
The Scope 2 Guidance requires dual reporting: a location-based figure using average grid factors and a market-based figure reflecting contractual instruments. Neither replaces the other.

title: ISO 14064-1:2018 six categories
facts: ISO 14064-1:2018 replaced the three-scope model with six categories: 1 direct emissions and removals, 2 imported energy, 3 transportation, 4 products used by the organisation, 5 use of products from the organisation, and 6 other sources.

Category 1 maps to Scope 1 and category 2 to Scope 2. Categories 3 to 6 together are Scope 3, split on a different principle — ISO groups all transportation into one category where the GHG Protocol spreads it across four Scope 3 categories.
The totals reconcile exactly; the presentation does not. Reporting under both means presenting one inventory two ways, not computing it twice.

title: Where ISO 14064-1 is stricter than the GHG Protocol
facts: ISO 14064-1:2018 requires an organisation to assess the significance of every indirect emission category and document its justification for anything excluded from the inventory.
That is a stronger obligation than the GHG Protocol's optional Scope 3. An inventory that satisfies the Corporate Standard by omitting Scope 3 does not satisfy ISO 14064-1.

Direct removals sit inside ISO category 1 alongside direct emissions, where the GHG Protocol handles removals separately — so a company with material removals shows a different category 1 than its Scope 1.

title: ISO 14064-3 verification
facts: ISO 14064-3:2019 specifies requirements for validating and verifying GHG statements: selecting the verifier, agreeing the level of assurance, and setting objectives, criteria and scope.

Two levels: limited assurance gives a negative-form conclusion — nothing came to the verifier's attention suggesting material misstatement; reasonable assurance gives a positive-form conclusion after more extensive procedures.
Materiality is commonly set at 5% for reasonable assurance, and it drives the nature, timing and extent of the verification work.

The GHG Protocol has no verification standard of its own, so a GHG Protocol inventory is typically verified against ISO 14064-3 or ISAE 3410 — the accounting standard and the assurance standard are separate choices.
